items.title: Cincinnati Zoo's famed Fiona the hippo dies days after eating a visitor’s hat
items.standfirst: Fiona, the hippo whose premature birth and fight for survival at the Cincinnati Zoo turned her into a global sensation nearly a decade ago, died Thursday from complications after swallowing a knit hat that was accidentally flung into her enclosure. clusters.title: Here Are the Senators Who Are Backing Van Hollen Over Schumer for Senate Majority Leader
clusters.neutral_headline: Battle to replace Schumer as Democratic Senate leader heats up

items.title: Here Are the Senators Who Are Backing Van Hollen Over Schumer for Senate Majority Leader
items.standfirst: Senator Chris Van Hollen has said that he has the support of about 15 of his colleagues in his challenge against Senator Chuck Schumer.
items.content: Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT) speaks during a news conference at the U.S. Capitol Building in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 10, 2026. —Anna Moneymaker—Getty ImagesSenator Chris Van Hollen has said that he has the backing of about 15 of his colleagues in his quest to challenge Senator Chuck Schumer for Senate Majority Leader. So far, only a few of them have publicly declared their support.The progressive Maryland lawmaker announced his intent to run for the role last week, saying that the results of the 2026 midterm elections show that “the American people called for change,” not just from President Donald Trump but also “a change for the status quo that isn’t working for people.”“It’s now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need new leadership,” Van Hollen said in a social media post. “This is not about any one person—it’s about answering the call of the American people. That is why I’m running for Senate Majority Leader.”It marks the first time in decades that the race for the Senate Democratic leadership will be contested.Read More: Van Hollen Puts AI at Center of His Challenge to SchumerVan Hollen’s bid for the role comes as some members of the Democratic Party have pushed for new leadership, claiming that Schumer is too open to compromise. Schumer’s supporters, though, have credited him with the party’s victories in this year’s midterms.Schumer has led Senate Democrats for nearly a decade, and has expressed confidence that he has the votes needed to secure the leadership role in the upper chamber.Here are the senators and senators-elect who have said that they’re supporting Van Hollen.Bernie SandersSenator Bernie Sanders of Vermont, an Independent who caucuses with Democrats, has publicly declared that he supports Van Hollen in the contest.“This election was about CHANGE. The Democratic Party must CHANGE. Now is the time to take on the oligarchs and fight for working families,” Sanders said in a post on X last week. “That is why I will be supporting Chris Van Hollen for Majority Leader.”Sanders, a Democratic socialist, previously indicated that he would not support Schumer’s bid for the role. “The time is now to deal with the need to create an economy that works for all, not just the people on top,” he said at a press conference last week. “Do I think Chuck has been leading in that direction? No.”Jeff MerkleySenator Jeff Merkley of Oregon said in a social media post last week that Van Hollen has his “full support for Majority Leader.” Merkley said that he has seen Van Hollen “rally support for the people against the powerful time and time again.”“Americans are desperate to restore government by and for the people, not the privileged and powerful. We need leadership that carries that responsibility in their heart and gut. @VanHollenForMD is that leader,” Merkley said in one post. “Politics as usual is unacceptable,” he continued in another. “The American people have given us the opportunity to deliver. Let’s seize the day and make it happen.”Elissa SlotkinIn a video she shared on social media on Thursday, Senator Elissa Slotkin of Michigan spoke about how she had repeatedly stressed the importance of “a new generation of leadership” within the Democratic Party, “particularly after the election we just had earlier this month.”“I think that message was sent loud and clear: the American public want a new generation, and they want big and bold ideas,” she said. “I’ve been clear as well that I don’t think that Senator Schumer is best positioned to be our next leader.”She said that she was “encouraged” that others, like Van Hollen, had thrown their hat in the Senate Majority Leader race, and offered him her support.“Because I’ve been clear that I wasn’t supporting Schumer, I will be supporting Chris Van Hollen,” she said.But she went on to say that, no matter who becomes the next Senate Majority Leader, “it’s going to be imperative for our leaders to demonstrate how they’re going to incorporate that next generation and what big and bold ideas specifically they’re going to put forward in the first 100 days.”Abdul El-SayedSenator-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan said in a social media post last week that he “called on” Van Hollen “to lead our caucus as a candidate back in April because he leads with courage and experience.” “We need both right now,” El-Sayed continued. “Which is why I’m proud to stand with him in his bid to lead our Senate majority.”At the Atlantic Summit on Tuesday, El-Sayed said that his backing of Van Hollen was “not against Senator Schumer; it’s more about being for Senator Van Hollen.”“He’s unique in the Senate caucus around two things he brings together. Number one, he understands how this place works,” El-Sayed said. “But he also has a willingness to take risk. And we need people who are willing to take legislative risk.”“Most senators don’t fly down to El Salvador for proof of life for somebody like Kilmar Abrego Garcia,” he continued, referring to when Van Hollen traveled to the Central American country last year to meet with Abrego Garcia, a Maryland resident who was deported by the Trump Administration even though a federal court order shielded him from removal proceedings.Peggy FlanaganSenator-elect Peggy Flanagan of Minnesota has also backed Van Hollen, reiterating many of the sentiments her other colleagues have expressed.“I think people are looking for fighters,” she told CNN earlier this week. “They want people who are going to take on the Trump Administration, but I think they’re also ready for new voices to be incorporated into this party.”She went on to praise Van Hollen for his response to Abrego Garcia’s deportation.“I’ve watched Senator Van Hollen lead with courage and conviction,” she told CNN. “I think so many people really started paying attention to Chris Van Hollen when he got on an airplane and went and visited Kilmar Abrego Garcia, who was detained and deported. And that kind of courage, that kind of bold leadership, I think is important.”Flanagan also said that she believes that Van Hollen will be able to “”bring together the new class of members and folks who’ve been there for a while to make sure that we remember who we’re fighting for.”

items.title: ‘We’ve Got Time’: Trump Suggests Iran War Will Continue Into 2027
items.standfirst: The President told news outlets that he was not rushing to make any major decisions about renewed fighting until January.
items.content: U.S. President Donald Trump boards Air Force One at Joint Base Andrews, Md., on Nov. 16, 2026. —Win McNamee—Getty ImagesPresident Donald Trump suggested he is putting off any major decisions on Iran until 2027, amid reports that he’s considering renewed major operations in the war that continues despite repeated promises that it’ll end soon.Speaking to Reuters on whether new major strikes are possible—the U.S. has engaged in limited strikes on Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz—Trump, who was en route to Washington following his trip to China, said, “Well, I’ll talk to you about it after the beginning of the year.” He added: “We’ve got time.”Trump made similar comments in other interviews. “We’ll see what happens after January 1st," the U.S. President told Fox News in an interview that aired on Thursday, just before his summit with China’s Xi Jinping and Russia’s Vladimir Putin. He also told Axios in a phone call Thursday that he was “not rushing into any decision” on Iran.The President initially promised that the war with Iran would only take weeks, but it has dragged on to nearly nine months, though major hostilities have subsided. Trump has previously said that the war would end immediately after the Nov. 3 midterm elections, but the impasse between Iran and the U.S. remained. And in the past weeks, he’s alternated between publicly threatening Tehran and holding off on authorizing new strikes at the request of American allies in the Gulf. Israel has reportedly tried to convince Trump of a new joint strike. The New York Times reported that the U.S. President is considering a new round of extensive military strikes on Iran, after Tel Aviv warned of Tehran’s “success in rebuilding its missile and drone arsenals and advancing its chemical and biological weapons programs.” Benjamin Netanyahu, the Israeli Prime Minister whose premiership is in limbo, is reportedly pushing for a four- to seven-day airstrike campaign on Iran.Axios reported, citing unnamed sources, that the White House sought input from the Pentagon and intelligence experts on how Iran would respond to the strike scenarios prepared by the U.S. military. Axios also reported that any U.S. campaign would involve Israel and could include strikes on Iran’s nuclear facilities such as Pickaxe Mountain, energy and other infrastructure, and Iranian military and civilian leaders. The U.S. midterm elections, in which Democrats won control of Congress as the American public largely rebuked Trump and the Republican Party following their handling of the Iran war and the economic fallout it caused, could complicate decisionmaking. Before the Nov. 3 elections, Trump said that Iran was willing to strike a deal, but after the GOP’s stunning losses, which Iranian leaders celebrated, the Administration’s messaging pivoted to maintaining economic sanctions and the blockade on Iran.Vice President J.D. Vance has blamed the war for the GOP’s election losses, but still appeared to defend the President’s foreign policy on Iran. The Vice President earlier said there was no difference between the President and members of his Administration on the war, but as Vance voiced his misgivings, Trump ordered the Vice President to shift his focus away from Iran diplomatic negotiations and toward domestic policies.Trump has a small window to push through further military action against Iran before the newly elected Democrats take office in January. On Thursday, the GOP-led U.S. Senate rejected a measure aimed at curbing the war.Trump addresses reported ‘dirty bomb’ threat In the interview with Fox News, Trump said he thinks people should not be alarmed by reports of a planned “dirty bomb” attack on Washington, D.C. A dirty bomb combines conventional explosives like dynamite with radioactive material. “If it does happen, we wipe them out,” Trump said.Trump acknowledged, however, that intelligence indicated Tehran is potentially interested in biological weapons. “Iran is looking at gases, looking at bio, because we’ve shut them out with the nuclear,” he said, referring to the damage that the U.S. has claimed it dealt to Iran’s nuclear facilities.Iran’s foreign ministry refuted Trump’s recent statements. “The allegations keep changing, but the underlying narrative remains disturbingly familiar,” spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei said in a post on X. “Once again, the world is apparently expected to suffer a bout of collective amnesia."Baqaei then referred to how the U.S. justified its invasion of Iraq in 2003, alleging that the government of the late Saddam Hussein was developing weapons of mass destruction, which subsequent investigations found to be untrue. “We find ourselves facing ominous new allegations,” Baqaei said, “and a narrative that appears to be following the same fraudulent script.”
